title: Stalker 2 studio is raffling keychains made from a shot-down Russian helicopter to raise funds for mine removal in the real-world Chornobyl Exclusion Zone
summary: Other prizes include patches, t-shirts, and game keys—GSC Game World hopes to raise at least $100,000 for the effort.
body: Stalker 2 studio GSC Game World has joined with Ukrainian charity United24 on a new fundraising initiative that aims to raise $100,000 to help fund efforts to remove mines and other explosive devices from the real-world Chornobyl Exclusion Zone. The Zone—the real one—was established in 1986 following the disaster at the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant. It's not quite as fanciful as the videogame counterpart but it is hazardous, and public access is restricted; as one of the most radioactively contaminated regions on the planet, it's also of considerable scientific interest. Facilities in the zone also require ongoing maintenance, which became a problem when Russian troops seized the Zone and power plant during the early days of the invasion of Ukraine. The troops withdrew a couple months later—some reportedly received "significant doses" of radiation during their time there—leaving behind mines and explosives that pose a significant hazard to returning workers and researchers: United24 says at least eight explosions have wounded or killed staff and soldiers since the Russian withdrawal. "Demining the Chornobyl Exclusion Zone is first and foremost about the safety of the people who w…

title: Final Fantasy 7 Revelation gets a release date and a proper look at its airship overworld, which is cool, if in danger of inducing open world fatigue
summary: The Remake trilogy's a long one.
body: If there's one thing that's become daunting about the modern RPG, it's the ballooning time investment. There's no better example than the Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy, a reimagining of a classic that has stretched itself out between three entire fully-fledged games. Final Fantasy 7 Revelation just had its release date dropped alongside a 10-minute gameplay deep dive during PlayStation's State of Play . In it, we got to see a closer look at the airship overworld. It's pretty dang impressive. Your airship'll let you zip around the open world in record time, showing you a charming mini-model of each zone—it's not one hundred percent seamless (there's a cutscene between choosing a landing spot and parachuting down that's doubtless there to disguise some loading) but the ability to parachute down anywhere is neat, and it feels like a modern-day realisation of what the classic airship overworld of older RPGs were trying to do. We saw this in practice in a couple of locations, including Wutai—wherein Yuffie was able to grapple hook to a nearby roof and have a roam around. And yet, despite how impressive this all looks, I can't help but feel a certain dread set in. I haven't played FF7 …

title: Alien: Isolation 2's Gamescom demo kept its cards close to its chest, but I'm definitely ready to be terrified again
summary: Just, you know, give me a minute to collect myself.
body: It's like seeing an old friend: the clanking in the vents over your head, the way the ribbed tail passes over objects with a thunk-ka-thunk-ka-thunk-ka-thunk , the head-within-a-head, the screaming. You are here, you are back, you have been impaled through the abdomen and killed. I have played perhaps 20 minutes of Alien: Isolation 2 at Gamescom 2026 and I can tell you this: it is certainly Alien: Isolation. There are some new wrinkles, though—where the first game was a strictly inside affair, stranding you on the space station Sevastopol, the second game sets you down planetside in an entirely new character's shoes. Fewer air vents, fewer vital systems shuddering to a halt; a lot more weather, a lot more space. You are Blake. Here are the two things to know about Blake: she is not Amanda Ripley—the first game's protagonist who did not feature at all in my time with Alien: Isolation 2—but she is Weyland-Yutani. Specifically, she's Weyland-Yutani management, and isn't that interesting? You're no working class hero. You're now in the shoes of a character who, in any Alien movie worth its salt, would likely reveal themselves as a villain and end up decapitated about 70% of the way th…

title: Onimusha on Steam Deck is the definition of 'playable': Surprisingly pleasant, so long as 30 fps isn't a dealbreaker
summary: Capcom flaunts the flexibility of the RE Engine again.
body: We're long past the days of assuming the Steam Deck can comfortably handle the new big-budget action game of the moment, but here's a nice surprise: Valve's handheld is not a bad way to play Onimusha: Way of the Sword. It's not quite the optimization darling that Resident Evil Requiem was earlier this year, but it's much better news than Monster Hunter Wilds or Dragon's Dogma 2. After testing Onimusha in its taxing Kyoto hub area, I'd add this to the win column for Capcom's proprietary engine. To set expectations: Onimusha is a stubbornly 30-40 fps game on Deck. It can get as high as the 50s and 60s in the right conditions—turning FSR 3.1.4 upscaling on while in corridor areas outside the main hub—but you will eventually shoot back down to the 30s when there's a lot of action on screen. So if you're of the mind that a lower, stable framerate is ultimately the most comfortable way to play a game, then you can confidently lock it at 30 fps and turn off the performance overlay. That's how I played a decent chunk of it over the last few days, pausing here and there to see which graphical bumps I could get away with. The default configuration cranks everything down to its lowest settin…

title: CD Projekt Red isn't 'planning to rely on AI making complete games', and will still be 'predominantly using people' for The Witcher 4 and beyond
summary: "I think everybody has to make those judgments on their own."
body: Generative AI in videogame development, despite the looming potentiality of a bubble popping , has continued to be a hot-button topic pelted at developers during earning calls, despite most of them recognising that there's not much use for it beyond mundane busywork. Sure, it's being used commonly , but rarely for the actual making of the videogame itself. Filling in the roles that procedural generation might or, like, resizing shoulderpads—or for "user preference analysis" . Not exactly the kind of stuff that revolutionises an industry, and certainly not enough to justify reducing labour en masse. This also seems to be the view of joint CD Projekt Red CEO Michał Nowakowski, who was asked such a question during an earnings conference yesterday, and once more found himself required to emphasise that they're using people to make videogames like The Witcher 4: "AI is definitely becoming a thing in games development as well. We are still predominantly using people and this is our plan—to make games where we're not walking away from that." title: Corsair HS35 v3 review
summary: A very affordable mid-range headset that pulls off everything with aplomb, offering no surprises whether good or bad.
body: If you skipped buying that coveted stick of RAM or 2 TB SSD this time last year, you must be feeling understandably morose. Most things are getting more and more expensive, but crucially, not all things. Components like headsets and gamepads conform to the fast antiquating dictum that, with time, value will rise while costs decrease. That's pretty much the case with the Corsair HS35 v3. At the level of raw specs at least, Corsair's new mid-range headset has a touch more to offer than the SteelSeries Arctic Nova 3X, which is our favourite mid-range gaming headset. It came bearing a $90 price tag at launch (though you wouldn't pay full price for it in 2026). Like the Arctis Nova 3X, the HS35 v3 has 2.4 GHz wireless connectivity, Bluetooth, and a wired option. It has a detachable mic, and reasonably comfortable memory foam ear cups. Both models have 50mm drivers and a 20Hz - 20kHz frequency response. But the HS35 v3 is 10 grams lighter and $10 cheaper. Shots fired! title: The Blood of Dawnwalker - best settings to tweak
summary: The recommended specs are a little over-generous so here are the settings I reckon you can compromise to gain some extra performance.
body: The Blood of Dawnwalker is a punishing game. And not just because of the divisive time-as-a-resource-to-be-managed side of things (or the almost impossible to resist desire to shift 'the' around in the title) but because it will slay your PC in terms of performance. We've covered the fact that in order to hit any of the performance level system requirements you have to enable upscaling in Balanced mode , but it's also worth noting that those system requirements are a little generous, too. I've been testing Dawnwalker for the past week or so, with a few different setups, and in those forests of Carpathia you're going to either need some more beefy hardware to hit Rebel Wolves' proposed frame rate targets or compromise on those graphics settings. Which is where I'm coming in here, aiming to help you get the highest frame rate out of your rig without sacrificing the actual look of the game. And, actually The Blood of Dawnwalker does pretty well even down at the lower end of the graphics settings, still looking relatively crisp and with a detailed open world for you to explore to your vampyric heart's content.
